answers.1: The main objects are: STE-80, a writing style for technical text; ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English), a standard for aircraft maintenance manuals; the manual reader, who reads under time pressure and often in a second language; one sample sentence from a manual; its word count, shown by the orange bar; and three rules: (1) use simple words, (2) give the instruction directly, (3) use a concrete verb. Full STE adds more rules: short sentences, one meaning per word, and an approved dictionary.
answers.2: STE-80 uses about 80% of the ASD-STE100 rules. The three rules are applied one after another to the same sentence, and the bar tracks the word count: 16 → 15 (rule 1) → 13 (rule 2) → 9 (rule 3). The reader's situation (time pressure, second language) is the reason every word must help. Full STE is the larger set, and STE-80 is a subset of it.
answers.3: The reader has little time and may not read English as a first language, so each word must help. The rules replace hard words, remove the 'it is imperative that…' frame and name the action with a verb. The result is a shorter sentence that gives the same instruction with less work to read.
answers.4: The video never names the most important variable, so I can only infer one. If 'word count' is that variable, cutting words lowers reading effort as long as the meaning stays the same ('the reader still fills the reservoir'). If 'reader pressure' (time, second language) is the variable, more pressure would make each unneeded word cost more. Neither cause-and-effect link is stated directly.
answers.5: Assumption or simplification: fewer words and simpler words mean 'less work to read'. The video asserts this and does not show it. Simplification: STE-80 keeps only about 80% of the rules, and the video shows only three. Fact: ASD-STE100 is a standard for aircraft maintenance manuals, and the sample sentence goes from 16 words to 9.
answers.6: STE-80 is a writing style that uses about 80% of the rules of ASD-STE100, a simplified English standard for aircraft maintenance manuals. Manual readers work under time pressure and often in a second language, so every word must help. Rule one swaps hard words for simple ones ('replenished prior to commencing' becomes 'full before starting'). Rule two removes the 'it is imperative that the operator ensures' frame and says 'make sure'. Rule three uses an action verb ('fill') and a concrete noun ('machine'), so the sentence drops from 16 words to 9 with the same meaning.
answers.7: Rule three was the hardest. The narration says 'make sure that it is full asks the reader to check a result', but it does not say why that is worse than naming the action. The transition frame at 68.27s also shows overlapping, garbled text ('Make sure the / machine. operation.'). Stating the cost of the 'check a result' wording, and a clean before/after with no overlap, would have made it easier.
answers.8: Rule one replaces 'replenished prior to commencing' (4 words) with 'full before starting' (3 words), so the count goes from 16 to 15. The video says it helps because 'each word is easier to read'. It does not say why simple words are easier. I can only connect this to the earlier point about second-language readers; the video does not make that link.
answers.9: Rule three removes the most: 13 → 9, which is four words. 'Make sure that … is full' becomes 'Fill', and 'the operation' becomes 'the machine'. Rule two removes two words (the frame 'It is imperative that the operator ensures' becomes 'Make sure … you start').
answers.10: The video does not answer this directly. Rule one hints that word count is not the only measure: 'Only one word goes, but each word is easier to read.' The conclusion still treats '16 became 9' as the result, and full STE lists 'short sentences' as a rule. So the video neither says nor rules out that shorter is always better. It never shows a case where cutting words hurts.

reasons.6: No deduction. The summary is accurate and specific with examples for each rule. It calls the result 'the same meaning' without noting the operation→machine change of reference, and it does not mention the missing dictionary check.
reasons.7: No deduction. The difficulty is specific and actionable: the unexplained cost of 'check a result' and the garbled overlapping frame at 68.27s.
reasons.8: No deduction. It states the swap from hard to simple words and the benefit that each word is easier to read. It does not frame the rule as shortening; 16→15 is given only as the count.
reasons.9: No deduction. It names rule three, 'make sure that … is full' → 'fill', 13→9. Its rule-two figure (two words, 15→13) differs from the expected 16→13, because model.md is internally inconsistent here.
reasons.10: Partial. The expected answer is 'No'. The reviewer says the video neither says nor rules out that shorter is always better. It does cite the rule-one hint ('only one word goes, but each word is easier'), but it never states that the target is less decoding with the same meaning.
